title: Common Core SL.CCR.4 Explained
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart explains the fourth Speaking and Listening anchor standard — presenting information so that listeners can follow the reasoning, with organization and style fitted to task, purpose and audience — and defends it against the charge that it is boring. His first argument is economic: there is almost no employment sector where the ability to give a clear, well-organized report is not valuable, and he uses his brother-in-law's experience as a new corporate hire to show what that looks like at entry level. His second argument is that the standard leaves enormous room for creativity, illustrated by Scott Harrison of Charity:Water, who redesigned the concept of a charity around a message simple enough to tweet. The unifying teaching idea is TAP — task, audience, purpose — which Stuart wants students analyzing habitually across K-12 for both writing and speaking tasks. The two examples bracket the range: the same TAP analysis tells one man to keep his reports short and clear and tells another to blow up the conventions of his field. The piece is a good illustration of Stuart's method of giving a dull-sounding standard a memorable nickname and a human exemplar.
points: Stuart's promotion argument: clear, easy-to-follow informational speaking is one of the few near-universally rewarded workplace skills, evidenced by his brother-in-law's boss wanting reports and comments rather than opinions from a new hire.
He resolves the 'this standard is boring' objection by showing that task and audience, not the standard, set the ceiling on creativity — an entry-level employee is constrained, a founder is not.

Scott Harrison and Charity:Water serve as his exemplar of the standard at full stretch: name, promotional materials and the 100%-of-public-donations funding model all carry one simple message and call to action.
The transferable classroom tool is TAP (task, audience, purpose), which he wants students applying habitually to every speaking and writing task, and task-and-purpose alone to reading and listening.
He explicitly links this standard back to the writing anchor standard W.CCR.4, arguing the same analytic habit should run across strands rather than being taught separately in each.
quotes: At its core, this standard is about speaking well in front of people on factual topics. The kind of speaking task it envisions seems pretty no-nonsense. Essentially, SL.CCR.4 seems to be saying, “Give an effective and informative report.

There are very few employment sectors where this skill isn't highly valuable and highly promotion-friendly. My brother-in-law recently began working at a new company, and he made a profound observation to me the other day: “My bosses don't want opinions on labor issues from a new guy like me; they want quick and easy-to-follow reports and comments.

Toward this end, Scott founded Charity:Water. From the organization's name (it's a charity for providing water) to its promotional materials (check out this video) to its fund allocation principles (100% of public donations go to charity work; admin costs are funded by a select group of private donors), Charity:Water maintains a simple and direct message and call to action.

I think TAP is something we want to put in front of our students again and again K-12. We want them to habitually analyze a writing or speaking task in terms of these three factors (or, for reading and listening tasks, for only task and purpose). It will make them efficient. It will make them effective.

In my broski's situation as a new employee in a big corporation, he needs to gain the respect of his superiors right now, and that requires that he keep presentations short, sweet, and clear, and that he do a great job at delivering consistent results and solving problems within his sandbox. Because he is cognizant of TAP, he's very likely to rise up the ol' ladder.
